name: Documented income earned in China (salary, fees, other current-account income)
eligibility: A 境外个人 with lawful current-account RMB income earned in China.
documents: Valid ID plus source-of-funds documents showing the transaction amount, including tax certificates (有交易额的购汇资金来源材料，含税务凭证).
cap: No amount limit in the rule for genuine, lawful current-account income.
pros: The standard route for a U.S. passport holder. One wire. The cheapest conversion route. No SAFE approval step.
cons: The bank will not proceed without tax evidence. If Chinese tax was never paid on the income it must be settled first, and that tax — not the transfer — is the large number.
tax: No tax on the conversion or the wire in any source read. PRC income tax applies to the underlying income if unpaid: 3-45% on comprehensive income, 20% flat on interest, dividends, rent and property gains.

name: Foreign currency already in your Chinese FX account
eligibility: You hold a foreign-currency account in China with dollars in it.
documents: Valid ID. No conversion, so no purchase documents.
cap: Not stated in the sources read.
pros: No conversion at all, so no 0.21% spread. Cheapest thing on the whole site: $32.42 on $10,000 and $61.28 on $400,000, whatever the amount.
cons: Only helps to the extent dollars are actually there. Moving CNY into the FX account first would be a conversion and would attract the spread.
tax: No conversion means no disposition of nonfunctional currency at the wire, so no §988 gain arises on the transfer. The basis column is left blank rather than guessed.

name: Annual USD 50,000 convenience amount on a Chinese Foreign Permanent Resident ID
eligibility: A 境外个人 who holds a 外国人永久居留身份证.
documents: The card alone, inside the annual amount. Above it, source-of-funds documents.
cap: USD 50,000 equivalent per person per year on ID alone. It is not a cap: above it you simply cannot proceed on ID alone.
pros: No document assembly inside the annual amount.
cons: A U.S. passport holder without the card does not qualify at all. Above USD 50,000 the balance has to be bought year by year, one wire and one telegraph charge each — $1,330.12 on $400,000 against $901.20 for a single wire.
tax: Same as M01 for the underlying income.

name: Emigrant property transfer (移民财产转移)
eligibility: A natural person who emigrated from the mainland and had a Chinese household registration that has been cancelled.
documents: Written application, the applicant form, ID, the hukou cancellation certificate and proof of settlement abroad certified by a Chinese embassy or consulate, property-right documents, and a tax payment certificate from the tax authority where the property sits.
cap: No amount ceiling. Approval sits with the SAFE branch at your former hukou location.
pros: Built for exactly this problem: the whole pre-emigration estate, converted and remitted. Since 2014 the bank may remit the approved amount in one lump, the RMB 500,000 head-office filing is cancelled, and notarisation of property documents and of the agency agreement is cancelled.
cons: Unavailable to a U.S. citizen who never held a Chinese hukou. Approval is a SAFE decision, not an entitlement, and no fee or service standard is published. Chinese tax must be settled before the hukou is cancelled.
tax: PRC tax on the underlying property gain (20% flat on property transfer) must be evidenced before approval.

name: Inheritance transfer (继承财产转移)
eligibility: A foreign citizen or HK/Macau resident who inherited property located in the mainland.
documents: Written application stating the relationship, the applicant form, ID with settlement-abroad proof, proof of inheritance, the decedent's property-right documents and a tax payment certificate from the tax authority where the property sits.
cap: No amount ceiling. Approval sits with the SAFE branch at the decedent's last hukou location.
pros: The right route when the money arrived by inheritance. Since 2014 several inheritances can be combined at one decedent's hukou location and notarisation is no longer required.
cons: The bank must remit straight to your own account abroad — no cash withdrawal in China. Property whose lawful source cannot be proven will not be accepted. Approval timelines are not published.
tax: PRC tax on the underlying property must be evidenced before approval.

name: Change unused RMB back with the original exchange slip
eligibility: You brought foreign currency in, converted it to RMB yourself, and still hold the exchange slip.
documents: Valid ID plus the original exchange slip.
cap: Not re-verified this pass — see flag N676-U09.
pros: Avoids the income-documentation route entirely where it applies.
cons: Depends on holding the slip and on the conversion being recent. Not verified this pass.
tax: No tax on the conversion itself in the sources read.

name: Wire to Hong Kong, Macau or Taiwan as a first leg
eligibility: Same as M01, with a receiving account in HK, Macau or Taiwan.
pros: The telegraph charge on that leg is RMB 80 instead of RMB 150 — about $10.46 cheaper per wire.
cons: It is only a first leg. The onward transfer to the U.S. is a second transfer with its own charges, none of them published here, and the intermediate stop may have its own reporting consequences.

name: Carrying banknotes across the border
eligibility: Anyone, within the limits SAFE and customs set.
cap: The limits are set by SAFE under Decree 532 art. 15 but the limits themselves were not re-read this pass.
cons: Carrying FX out in breach draws a warning and a fine of up to 20% of the amount. On the U.S. side the declaration threshold and the form were not re-read this pass. At these amounts this route is not competitive with a wire and carries real seizure risk.
tax: No conversion tax. Reporting failures are the exposure.

name: Dividend from your own Chinese company
eligibility: The money is inside a Chinese company you own.
documents: Board profit-distribution resolution and the tax filing form (税务备案表) above USD 50,000.
cap: The USD 50,000 figure here is an institutional document-review threshold, NOT the individual convenience amount.
pros: A genuine route where the money is corporate.
cons: Entirely different question from the personal routes: corporate income tax first, then 20% dividend tax, then the remittance. Needs a corporate adviser.
tax: 20% individual income tax on dividends, on top of corporate tax already paid.

name: Borrowing relatives' or friends' annual amounts ('ant moving')
pros: None. It is not a route.
cons: SAFE treats quota splitting as evasion. The people involved go on a watch list for the year of listing and the following two years, during which every conversion needs transaction documents. Fines run to 30% of the amount, 30-100% in serious cases, with criminal liability possible.

name: Private swaps, money changers, false invoices, crypto
pros: None. It is not a route.
cons: Art. 45 covers private buying and selling, disguised dealing, reselling and illegally brokering FX: confiscation of illegal gains, fines up to 30%, 30-100% in serious cases, and criminal liability. Art. 40 covers buying FX on false documents.

name: Leaving the balance in China
cons: The U.S. reporting obligations do not stop because the money did not move. FBAR and Form 8938 apply to the account itself, with maxima of $16,536 and $165,353 per violation.
tax: No conversion, so no §988 gain now — but the gain is deferred, not avoided.
